q-123371.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14196541/assets/5b6490495c297b49d394b0f7c494fb35b710c8c4520ab898783877abdd079013.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=2-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi ,$ shown above?
q-123371.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=2-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{(2-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{4-16\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +16{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +16{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{4-16\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +16}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{20-16\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{5-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

q-123371.html:
Question 1
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cds, where C is the path along the polar curve r=2−4sin⁡θ for π2≤θ≤π, shown above?

a
2∫π/2π4−5cos⁡θdθ
b
2∫π/2π5−4sin⁡θdθ
c
∫π/2π5−4sin⁡θdθ
d
2∫π/2π5−4cos⁡θdθ
e
2∫π/2π5+4cos⁡θdθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over C is equal to the arc length L of C, i.e., ∫Cds=L.

In polar coordinates, the arc length element ds is given by

ds=r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

So, for a polar curve defined as r=r(θ) for θ1≤θ≤θ2, we have

L=∫Cds=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=2−4sin⁡θ, we have drdθ=−4cos⁡θ.

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

∫Cds=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫π/2π(2−4sin⁡θ)2+(−4cos⁡θ)2dθ=∫π/2π4−16sin⁡θ+16sin2⁡θ+16cos2⁡θdθ=∫π/2π4−16sin⁡θ+16dθ=∫π/2π20−16sin⁡θdθ=2∫π/2π5−4sin⁡θdθ.

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=4+\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta \,$ for $-\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{7\pi }{6},$ shown above?
q-123395.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=4+\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\sqrt{(4+\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta )^{2}+(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta )^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\sqrt{16+8\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡4\theta +16{sin}^{2}⁡4\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\sqrt{16+8\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta +1+15{sin}^{2}⁡4\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\sqrt{17+8\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta +15{sin}^{2}⁡4\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}

q-123634.name: Question 3
q-123634.problem: Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\sqrt{2}\,{e}^{\theta }\,$ for $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$
q-123634.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\sqrt{2}{e}^{\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=\sqrt{2}\,{e}^{\theta }.
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(\sqrt{2}\,{e}^{\theta })}^{2}+{(\sqrt{2}\,{e}^{\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{2{e}^{2\theta }+2{e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{4{e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}2{e}^{\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{e}^{\theta }{|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2} \\  & =2({e}^{\pi /2}-{e}^{\pi /4}) \\  & =2{e}^{\pi /4}({e}^{\pi /4}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

q-123643.name: Question 4
q-123643.problem: Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\sqrt{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }\,$ for $\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi .$
q-123643.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\sqrt{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }\,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{\sqrt{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}.
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{(\sqrt{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta })^{2}+{(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{\sqrt{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }})}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )+\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡2\theta }{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{\frac{(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )^{2}+{cos}^{2}⁡2\theta }{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{\frac{1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡2\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡2\theta }{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\sqrt{\frac{2-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}\,\theta {|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =\sqrt{2}\text{ }(\pi -\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}

q-149800.name: Question 5
q-149800.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\frac{1}{\theta }$ for $1\le \theta \le \pi \,?$
q-149800.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\frac{1}{\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-\frac{1}{{\theta }^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\pi }\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{\theta })}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{{\theta }^{2}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\pi }\sqrt{\frac{1}{{\theta }^{2}}+\frac{1}{{\theta }^{4}}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\pi }\sqrt{\frac{{\theta }^{2}+1}{{\theta }^{4}}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\pi }\frac{\sqrt{{\theta }^{2}+1}}{{\theta }^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cds, where C is the path along the polar curve r=1θ for 1≤θ≤π?

a
∫1πθ2+12θdθ
b
∫1πθ4+1θ2dθ
c
∫1πθθ+1dθ
d
∫1πθ2+1θ2dθ
e
∫1π2θθ2+1dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over C is equal to the arc length L of C, i.e., ∫Cds=L.

In polar coordinates, the arc length element ds is given by ds=r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

So, for a polar curve defined as r=r(θ) for θ1≤θ≤θ2, we have L=∫Cds=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=1θ, we have
drdθ=−1θ2.

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is ∫Cds=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫1π(1θ)2+(−1θ2)2dθ=∫1π1θ2+1θ4dθ=∫1πθ2+1θ4dθ=∫1πθ2+1θ2dθ.
